newsitem.title: USA: Fort James combination seen as outperformer.
newsitem.headline: Fort James combination seen as outperformer.

text.p: Shareholders of James River Corp and Fort Howard Corp have approved a $5.8 billion merger that will create the world's second-largest tissue producer, a combination that analysts said should outperform the industry.
The new company, Fort James Corp, will have annual sales of more than $7 billion, with brands such as Quilted Northern bathroom tissue, Brawny paper towels, Vanity Fair napkins and Dixie paper cups.

"It's a very logical, positive merger in an industry that has been hurt by fragmentation," Kathryn McAuley, an analyst with Brown Brothers Harriman & Co in New York, said Tuesday. "The Street is welcoming consolidation."

The deal, expected to close Wednesday, calls for Fort Howard shareholders to receive 1.375 James River shares for each Fort Howard share they hold. The transaction, including the assumption of Fort Howard debt, was valued at $5.8 billion when it was announced May 5.

Investors have welcomed the merger, with James River and Fort Howard shares touching a fresh 52-week highs on Tuesday. James River has risen about 45 percent and Fort Howard about 69 percent since the agreement was unveiled.
Later in the afternoon, James River closed at 43-1/4, down 11/16 on the day, and Fort Howard shed 1-7/16 to 58-15/16. During the session, the overall market sagged amid rising bond yields.
Fort James is likely to "outperform the industry as a whole," McAuley said. She recently raised her 12-month price target for Fort James shares to $52 from $44 in May.
"What I am looking for is steady growth and synergies," she said, adding she based the price target on her projection of earnings of about $2.75 a share in 1998.
"The price target is a market multiple of 19 times, but (Fort James) could trade at a premium, too," she said.
McAuley likes the synergies the merger would create. James River said in May the merger allow for cost-cutting of at least $150 million in 1998 and more in coming years.
"There's a possibility (the company) will achieve more than that," she said.
The combined company's $4.4 billion debt is the only potential wrinkle, McAuley said.

"James River will be very active to refinance Fort Howard's high-yield debt," she said, adding Fort Howard's $1.6 billion debt is left over from the company's leverageed buyout in the 1980s. McAuley said the company's strong cash flow should reduce the burden by $1.2 billion by 2000.
Josh Kapp, an analyst with Smith Barney, said the debt load probably would not affect the company's earnings, which he projects at $2.80 a share in 1998.
"We came up with a pretty good cash flow (of Fort James), over $500 million in 1998," Kapp said, adding he expects the company to earn $0.55 in the third quarter and $0.50 in the fourth quarter.
A July 24 First Call survey of 10 analysts put Fort James earnings at $0.54 a share in the third quarter, $0.51 a share in the fourth quarter, and $2.58 a share in 1998.
McAuley said Fort James, which will stand as the world's second-largest tissue products maker after Kimberly Clark Corp, will derive 80 percent of its $7 billion in annual sales from tissue products.
With the merger between James River and Fort Howard thinning the ranks of the paper products industry, Kapp said he expected further consolidation, but not necessarily companies gobbling up others.
"We'll see some asset swaps, but that won't necessarily change the number of companies in the industry," Kapp said.
